title: Pluto Seen up Close for the First Time

paragraphs.text: NASA has released images taken when a space probe, a small rocket equipped with a camera, passed closely by Pluto, a planet in the outer reaches of the solar system. Pluto is often referred to as a ‘dwarf planet’ because of its small size. Until this mission, it had never been seen so close-up and with such precision, and little was known about it. The space probe, New Horizons, passed within 8,000 miles of the frozen world.

The images include a high-resolution view of a small area near Pluto’s equator, in which mountains made of water ice rise 11,000 feet above what appears to be a young, active surface. Charon, Pluto’s largest moon, has also emerged in surprising detail. And then there’s the first image of Hydra, one of the system’s four small moons. Already, these images are challenging views about how small, icy worlds work. ‘I think the whole system is amazing,’ said New Horizons principal investigator Alan Stern. ‘This system is something wonderful.’

As data taken in deep space was sent back to Earth, which took a total of 16 months, the team began to dig through this. The first observations included information about both Pluto’s atmosphere and what the planet is made of, as well as the system’s four small moons. A New World Initial data showed that Pluto is a spotty world that doesn’t resemble anything else in the solar system – even if its reddish hue does somewhat suggest Mars. New Horizons also found that Pluto is bigger than we thought.

Pluto’s surface, little understood for 85 years, is unique. The world is covered in dramatically different terrains, some smooth, some with large craters, deep depressions in the ground. The new Pluto images reveal a portion of the planet with large mountains looming over a surface that looks relatively young – so young, in fact, that it suggests the planet is still geologically active.

‘We have not yet found a single impact crater on this image,’ said team member John Spencer. ‘Pluto has been bombarded by other objects in the Kuiper Belt**. Craters happen. We think it has to be probably less than 100 million years old… it might be active right now.’
Pluto also varies in brightness. Near the planet’s equator is an extremely bright, heart-shaped region the team is now informally calling Tombaugh Region, after the man who discovered Pluto in 1930.

‘We could see the heart very far from Pluto,’ Stern said. ‘You could see that shining like a beacon, and because it’s the brightest and most prominent feature on the planet, that’s why we want to call it Tombaugh Region.’

The heart’s halves appear to be made from different ingredients, with one side being very smooth and the other more mountainous. Studying its boundaries should provide more information about what’s going on, and whether the smoother terrains are elevated or sunken. Around the heart on either side are spots that are about as dark as anything can get. Images from the New Horizons probe have not given good clues as to the make-up of the surrounding area. Pluto’s Many Moons Charon, Pluto’s largest moon, is just over half the size of the planet it orbits. This is large enough that some would consider it another dwarf planet, in a two-planet, or binary, system orbiting each other. They spin around a point in the space between them, continuously floating opposite each other. Charon looks dramatically different from Pluto. While scientists expected Charon to be intriguing, they weren’t prepared for the image that came back.

‘It’s a small world with deep canyons, cliffs, and dark regions that are still slightly mysterious to us,’ said deputy project scientist Cathy Olkin. ‘There is so much interesting science going on in this image alone.’ Charon has a mysterious dark pole that could be made of materials that escaped from Pluto. Team members are informally referring to that area as Mordor.

The moon is also cracked – and some of those cracks are enormous, as much as five or six miles deep. What’s more, Charon’s surface is not ancient and completely cratered, as scientists had anticipated. Instead, it contains few craters, suggesting that it might also be an active world.

Scientists think Charon formed from a giant collision with Pluto while it was itself forming, and that debris from this eventually created the pair’s four smaller moons, called Nix, Hydra, Kerberos, and Styx.

Hydra has now been seen for the first time, though the photos are dim and blurry. But team members figured out that the moon is 27 miles long. ‘The surface of Hydra is surprisingly large,’ says project scientist Hal Weaver. ‘That can only mean that Hydra’s surface is probably composed primarily of water ice.’
Altogether, the Pluto system is like a tiny, complex planetary system, and scientists hope that by unlocking Pluto’s secrets, they’ll learn more about how planetary systems form and evolve.
